analysis.one_liner: Raises average new-car fuel economy to 33 miles per gallon and allows makers to trade efficiency credits.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan House bill to require 33 mpg average fuel economy by 2017 died in subcommittee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have directed the Transportation Department to set fuel economy standards so that cars made after 2016 average at least 33 miles per gallon, cutting the oil used by U.S. cars by about 10 percent starting in 2017. It let the Department set separate standards by vehicle size and create a credit-trading program so a maker that beat the standard could sell credits to one that fell short. It also told regulators not to degrade vehicle safety and to protect U.S. auto manufacturing jobs.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers, who would save money at the gas pump as new vehicles became more efficient, and the country as a whole through reduced oil consumption beginning in 2017. The bill included safeguards requiring that safety not be degraded and that U.S. auto manufacturing jobs be maximally retained.

how_it_helps.text: Requires standards ensuring automobiles made after 2016 average at least 33 miles per gallon, with the goal of cutting U.S. automobile fuel use by 10 percent beginning in 2017 [S2] [S3].

Allows the Secretary to set separate standards for different size classes of vehicles, and to let manufacturers that beat the standard sell credits to manufacturers that miss it, easing compliance [S2] [S3].
Directs that fuel economy improvements not degrade vehicle safety and that the standards maximize retention of U.S. auto manufacturing jobs [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Automakers, who would bear the cost of engineering more efficient vehicles, likely passed on partly to new-car buyers through higher prices; and the oil industry, which would sell roughly 10 percent less fuel for cars once the goal took effect.

drawbacks.text: Tougher standards raise compliance costs for manufacturers, which likely translates into higher prices for new vehicles, hitting buyers of new cars first [S3].

Higher fuel economy historically pushed manufacturers toward smaller, lighter vehicles, a tradeoff the bill tried to address by directing that safety not be degraded and by allowing separate standards by vehicle size — but whether regulators could actually deliver both efficiency and safety would depend on how the rules were written [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer savings from lower fuel use and the reduction in oil consumption were substantial and would have arrived by 2017, while the main costs — engineering expense and somewhat higher new-car prices — were borne gradually and by a narrower group. The bill was also built with industry-friendly flexibility (size-based standards, credit trading, job-retention and safety criteria), which made the tradeoff more manageable than a flat mandate. On balance the benefits outweighed the costs, though the burden on manufacturers was real.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Energy and Air Quality subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended — no hearing, no vote, nothing.

narrative.text: Representative David Reichert, a Republican from Washington State, introduced the bill on January 24, 2007, joined by 12 original cosponsors [S3].
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S5].
On February 2, 2007, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality, where no further action was taken for the rest of the 110th Congress [S5].
The bill attracted 18 cosponsors — 15 Republicans and 3 Democrats — but never reached the House floor [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers and oil companies were better off because the bill died: no 33 mpg mandate, no redesign costs, and no 10 percent cut in gasoline demand. Drivers kept paying for the fuel the standards would have saved.

for.name: Rep. David Reichert
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to raise fuel economy standards to 33 mpg and reduce automobile oil use by 10 percent.

for.name: 18 House cosponsors (15 Republicans, 3 Democrats)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan support in both parties.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. John Dingell (D-MI), whose Michigan district centered on the auto industry
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a markup or vote; it sat in subcommittee until the Congress ended.

against.name: U.S. auto industry
against.role: Automobile manufacturers subject to fuel economy standards
against.what_they_did: Consistently opposed tougher federal fuel economy mandates during this era, arguing they raised costs and burdened domestic manufacturers.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and 15 of 18 cosponsors were Republicans, with 3 Democrats joining; the bill died in committee before any vote could show how the chambers really split.

industries.note: The bill would have forced redesigns toward 33 mpg vehicles, raising compliance costs. Its interest ran against drivers' fuel savings, though the bill softened the blow with credit trading, size-based standards, and job-retention language.
A 10 percent cut in automobile fuel use beginning in 2017 means less gasoline sold. The industry's loss was the consumer's and country's gain.
Buyers would face somewhat higher new-vehicle prices but would recoup them through lower fuel spending over the vehicle's life.
